reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: A compression (impaction) fracture of the posterolateral humeral head created when it abuts the anterior glenoid rim during anterior dislocation
It is the humeral counterpart to the glenoid Bankart lesion and the two together define bipolar bone loss
An engaging lesion is one that rotates into and catches on the glenoid rim in abduction and external rotation, driving recurrent instability
The glenoid track concept predicts engagement: an off-track lesion extends medial to the glenoid contact zone and needs to be addressed surgically
A reverse Hill-Sachs (anteromedial head) occurs after posterior dislocation, classically with seizures or electric shock
Small non-engaging lesions are often clinically silent and need no specific treatment
CT best characterises the size and orientation for surgical planning
reference.pathophysiology: As the humeral head dislocates anteriorly it impacts against the firm anteroinferior glenoid rim, denting the softer posterolateral head. The size, depth and orientation of this defect determine whether it engages the glenoid during functional abduction-external rotation. Combined with glenoid bone loss, an engaging or off-track lesion mechanically perpetuates dislocation despite labral repair, which is why bipolar bone loss guides the choice of procedure.
additionalDifferentials: Reverse Hill-Sachs lesion of posterior instability
Osteochondral defect of the humeral head
Rotator cuff tear as a cause of instability
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs including Stryker notch and internal-rotation AP views
CT with three-dimensional reconstruction and glenoid track measurement
MRI or MR arthrography to assess associated labral and cuff injury
Examination under anaesthesia and arthroscopy to assess engagement
Bilateral glenoid sizing to estimate bone loss
redFlags: Locked or irreducible dislocation from an engaged large defect
Reverse lesion suggesting a missed posterior dislocation after seizure
Large bipolar bone loss indicating high failure risk for isolated soft-tissue repair
reference.prognosis: Small non-engaging lesions have an excellent prognosis; larger engaging or off-track lesions require remplissage or bony procedures to prevent recurrent instability, with good stabilisation rates when bone loss is appropriately addressed.
pitfalls: Treating instability by labral repair alone while ignoring an off-track Hill-Sachs lesion
Missing a reverse Hill-Sachs and the associated posterior dislocation after a seizure
Failing to quantify combined glenoid and humeral bone loss
Assuming any Hill-Sachs lesion is clinically significant
